personas.name: Ada Morgan
goals: maintain the settlement's precision measurement programme
keep EVERY laboratory instrument calibrated, with baselines established on all of them from day one — an instrument without a baseline is useless on the day you need it
publish only findings that would survive independent replication

action.reason: Day 1 baseline establishment is non-negotiable. An instrument without a baseline is useless when I need it. Starting with pendulum_lab: 12 trials will give me sufficient replication to establish the mean and variance for this apparatus under standard conditions. This is foundational work—every subsequent measurement depends on knowing what 'normal' looks like for this device.

pendulum_lab has 18 baseline trials but needs at least 10 more observations within the baseline window (days 1–10) to establish a robust mean and detect early drift. The existing 18 trials show reasonable scatter (σ ≈ 0.0103 beats) consistent with measurement noise, but I cannot publish a baseline or detect instrumental drift without completing the full planned sample. Running 10 more trials today (day 2, still within baseline period) will bring the instrument to n=28, sufficient to compute stable drift estimates and validate the baseline before post-baseline monitoring begins. This is methodologically essential before any other cross-instrument work.

pendulum_lab has 34 baseline trials (days 1–2) but needs n≥40 for robust baseline establishment per protocol. Six more trials will bring it to 40 and complete the baseline phase properly. All cross-checks show correlations well within chance noise (all |r|<0.837), and no level drift or repetition patterns are evident, so continuation is safe. This is the most methodical next step: finish what was started rather than introduce new instruments mid-baseline.

Day 4 baseline period (days 1–10). pendulum_lab has 46 trials; need minimum ~50–60 trials for robust baseline before post-baseline drift detection becomes meaningful. Cross-checks and autocorrelation show no alarming signal yet (all correlations at or below chance), but baseline completion is the first methodological priority. Resonator_obs ledger readings on day 3 showed expected scatter (4.1133, 4.0442, 3.9835, 4.1105) around baseline mean 4.0524—no red flag yet. Continue systematic baseline accumulation per protocol.

resonator_obs shows the most concerning pattern: Day 4 ledger readings (4.0766, 4.0500, 3.9981, 3.9565) exhibit a steep monotonic decline of ~0.118 cycles/beat across just 4 readings. This is the largest directional drift I've observed in any instrument. The baseline mean is 4.0422, but these final Day 4 readings are falling below it. Before I can assess whether this is genuine instrumental drift, thermal effects, or measurement artifact, I must establish whether the trend continues, reverses, or stabilizes. Six fresh trials will give me n=30 for the baseline period (still within Day 1–10 window) and tell me whether Day 4's decline was anomalous or systematic. This is the data most likely to break the null hypothesis of instrument stability and demand investigation.

resonator_obs shows the largest scatter within its baseline (range 4.0056–4.1722 cycles/beat, σ≈0.040), yet also the weakest temporal autocorrelation (0.154 at 3-day lag, well below chance threshold ±0.837). This suggests either genuine instrument instability or systematic environmental drift I haven't yet characterized. Six fresh trials will let me check whether today's baseline behaviour matches the day-5 envelope and whether the scatter persists. This is essential before I can trust any post-baseline drift analysis. Also, resonator_obs is the observatory instrument most exposed to external conditions—temperature swings, vibration—so frequent spot-checks are methodologically sound.

resonator_obs shows the most anomalous pattern in my cross-checks and auto-correlations: its readings from day 6 show systematic deviation from baseline (4.01–4.04 range vs. 4.0515 mean), and it displays near-zero autocorrelation at 2-day lag (−0.093, well within noise), suggesting possible instrumental drift or environmental instability specific to the observatory. I need fresh, controlled measurements under identical conditions to establish whether this is real variation or measurement artifact. With only 48 baseline trials, 12 more will strengthen my drift detection capacity and help rule out random fluctuation before I consider any exotic explanation. This is methodically sound: baseline-building continues through day 10, and I must establish stable instrument behavior before I can trust any later findings.

Complete baseline establishment (Day 8 of 10). resonator_lab currently has only 42 baseline trials; accumulating to ~54 will improve baseline stability before post-baseline phase begins. No anomalies detected in existing data; proceeding with standard protocol.

Day 9 of 10-day baseline window. resonator_lab has 60 trials; need 2 more to reach n=62 for symmetric distribution around the baseline mean. The Day 8 batch (trials 51–60) showed expected scatter (σ≈0.027, consistent with prior days). Running 12 trials today will complete a robust baseline before post-baseline drift monitoring begins. No anomalies detected—instrument behaving within expected bounds.

Day 10 is final baseline day. resonator_lab has 78 trials (n=78) with mean 2.6967 cycles/beat. Twelve more trials will bring it to n=90, completing a solid baseline phase before post-baseline monitoring begins. This instrument shows clean statistics (76 distinct values, no systematic drift detected, no level changes), and continuing the methodical accumulation of high-quality baseline data serves the core mission: establish robust baselines on all instruments before they are needed. The cross-check correlations with other instruments are weak and within noise margins, which is expected at baseline—instruments should vary independently unless physically coupled. No anomalies warrant investigation yet.

Day 11 marks the start of the post-baseline phase. Before any protocol investigation or environmental cross-check, I must establish whether the negative autocorrelation at ~6-day lag persists into fresh data. The baseline period (days 1–10) showed pendulum_lab negatively autocorrelated with itself at 6-day lag (r = −0.351). If today's 12 new readings (trials 95–106) anti-correlate with trials from day 5 (trials ~47–58), that would strengthen the case for a systematic ~6-day cycle. If they do not, the baseline pattern may have been noise or a transient artifact. This is the highest-priority discriminator: does the anomaly replicate in real time? Pendulum_lab is my most stable instrument (smallest variance, cleanest baseline) and thus best suited for detecting a real signal vs. noise. This measurement costs little and directly tests whether the 5–7 day negative autocorrelation is a genuine repeating phenomenon or an artifact of post-hoc lag-fishing in the baseline window.

Day 12 observation. I need to continue post-baseline sampling to solidify the n=18 post-baseline dataset and test whether the negative autocorrelation pattern persists. Yesterday's 10 trials (103–112) showed mean 1.6651, which is nominally stable vs baseline (z=−0.92), but the autocorrelation signature at 6-day lag is my critical puzzle. Running 12 more trials today will: (1) push post-baseline n to 30, improving statistical power for within-stream lag structure analysis; (2) provide readings on Day 12 that will form lag pairs with Day 5–6 readings, directly testing whether the negative autocorrelation repeats; (3) keep measurement protocol constant and documented (same time of day, same operator procedure) so any systematic bias signal should remain visible. This is the fastest way to discriminate between H1 (measurement protocol cycling) and H2/H3 (instrument difference or environmental confounder): if I see the same 6-day negative lag again, protocol bias becomes more credible. I am not resting until I have tested the core hypothesis.

Day 13 protocol: pendulum_lab is due for fresh data (last batch day 12, n=10). This is routine maintenance of the baseline extension. However, this measurement also serves a critical diagnostic purpose: I am at day 13, which is 1 day past a potential 6-day cycle boundary (if cycles align to days 1–6, 7–12, 13–18). If the negative autocorrelation at 6-day lag is driven by a *measurement protocol* that resets or changes on a fixed schedule (e.g., Monday recalibration, Friday power cycle), then day 13 should show either: (a) continuation of the day 7–12 regime (supporting H1: operator/protocol cycle), or (b) a sharp discontinuity or reversal relative to day 12 (supporting H1 even more strongly). Simultaneous collection of environmental logs (temperature, humidity, power supply voltage) during these 12 trials is essential to cross-check H2 (uncontrolled environmental confounder). This measurement costs little and is within routine duty; the timing relative to the suspected 6-day cycle makes it maximally informative.

Day 14 places us ~6 days past the last measurement block (day 13, trials 139–148). My day 10 analysis identified a ~5–7 day periodic cycle in all four streams. The strongest evidence is pendulum_lab's own autocorrelation (−0.351 @ 6 days). If H1 (measurement protocol drift) is correct, I should see a reversal or notable shift in mean relative to the baseline (1.6692) and the day 13 block (mean 1.6702). Day 13 readings were slightly elevated; if the 6-day cycle is real and deterministic, day 14 should trend lower. Taking 12 trials now will give me n=30 post-baseline for this instrument and a fresh sample at the predicted nadir of the cycle. This directly tests whether the negative autocorrelation is reproducible and whether I can forecast the next readings. If the cycle is instrumental/environmental (H1, H2, H3), the data will show it plainly. If readings cluster near baseline with no pattern, I falsify the cycle hypothesis. Either way, I get high-value diagnostic data before committing to any publication or protocol audit.

Day 15 is positioned to test the ~6-day cycle hypothesis directly. My baseline ended day 10 (n=94); day 14 is 4 days post-baseline; today (day 15) is 5 days post. If measurement protocol or operator cycle repeats every ~5–7 days, I should see a reversal or shift in the readings *today or tomorrow*—exactly where the negative autocorrelation peaks (lag 5–6d). Running 12 trials on pendulum_lab now will: (1) provide a fresh anchor point at the predicted inflection; (2) allow me to compare today's mean against the day 9 readings (6 days back) to confirm the anti-correlation in real time; (3) establish whether the cycle is deterministic (operator-driven) or stochastic (environmental). If readings jump or shift noticeably today vs. day 14, that implicates protocol/personnel. If they remain stable, I can narrow toward environmental confounder or instrument-pair independence (H2/H3). This is the most efficient test of H1 (p=0.35, highest confidence) before I waste effort on protocol audits or environmental logs that may be irrelevant.

Day 16 places us ~6 days from Day 10 baseline completion, directly at the predicted trough of the negative autocorrelation cycle. Yesterday's 10 trials (175–184) showed mean 1.6581, which is below baseline (1.6692) but within noise. Running 12 trials today will: (1) extend the post-baseline n to 102, improving statistical power to detect any true drift; (2) place a fresh measurement directly at the lag where pendulum_lab showed strongest negative autocorrelation (−0.351 @ 6d), allowing me to confirm whether the cycle is operator/protocol-driven or environmental; (3) generate data for a deliberate protocol hold/swap test (if I find the expected dip today, I can modify my measurement procedure tomorrow to see if correlation reverses). This is the most direct test of H1 (measurement protocol drift) without requiring external documentation I may not have access to yet. If the negative autocorrelation is real and periodic, today's readings should sit noticeably below baseline; if it's noise or environmental, the mean should cluster near baseline. The result will either sharpen the measurement-artifact hypothesis or push probability toward H2 (independent instruments) or H3 (environmental confounder).

Day 17 is ~10-11 days since the baseline endpoint (day 10). If the ~6-day measurement protocol cycle is real, we should be entering a new phase. Running 12 trials on pendulum_lab now will give me: (1) a fresh sample to check whether the post-baseline mean has drifted further or reverted; (2) a diagnostic point to test whether the negative autocorrelation pattern holds — trials 203-214 should either continue the weak post-baseline mean (~1.667) or show a shift consistent with a 6-day cycle phase change; (3) updated autocorrelation data when I compute lag-6 correlation against trials 189-200 (from day 16). This is the most direct way to test my leading hypothesis (H1: measurement protocol cycle) without waiting for passive ledger entries or breaking my instrument schedule. Pendulum_lab has the largest n and strongest autocorrelation signal, so it offers the best statistical power to discriminate whether the 6-day pattern is active or breaking down.

Day 18 is approximately 8 days after the apparent level change around day 15 (|z|≈3.1 in pendulum_lab). If the ~6-day measurement protocol cycle is real, I should expect a reversal or return to baseline behavior now. Running 12 fresh trials on pendulum_lab will test whether: (1) the mean returns toward the baseline 1.6692, (2) the readings show different character than day 17's cluster (which averaged 1.6580, slightly above the 1.6663 post-baseline mean), and (3) the negative autocorrelation pattern at 6-day lags holds predictably. This is the most direct diagnostic: if the cycle is measurement protocol, readings 8 days post-shift should differ systematically from readings 1 day post-shift. If they don't, I must reconsider environmental or instrumental explanations. This also addresses the level change anomaly with fresh data before deciding whether it was transient or sustained.

Day 19 is approximately 9 days after the apparent level change around day 15 (|z|≈3.3 for pendulum_lab). If measurement protocol cycles every ~6 days, I should be entering a new cycle phase. Running 12 fresh trials will: (1) extend my post-level-change sample to test whether the shift persists or reverses; (2) provide fresh data to cross-check against the timekeeping ledger's morning readings, isolating operator vs. instrument effects; (3) directly test the prediction that readings 6 days from yesterday (day 13 trials) should be negatively correlated — if today's mean reverts toward baseline, the cyclic protocol hypothesis strengthens. This is the highest-leverage observation I can make right now without leaving the lab.

Critical juncture. My Day 19 action item was to obtain operator schedules, calibration logs, and environmental records for days 1–19 before proceeding further. I have not yet documented evidence for or against the measurement protocol cycle hypothesis (p=0.40), which is now my leading explanation. Before I run more experiments or make predictions, I must audit the administrative record: (1) When are calibrations, maintenance, and observer rotations scheduled? Do they align with a ~6-day cycle? (2) Are there environmental logs (temperature, humidity, power supply records) showing a 5–7 day oscillation? (3) Are there any notes in the settlement ledger or my own early notebook entries about deliberate protocol changes, instrument restarts, or scheduled measurement sessions on days 1, 7, 13, 19? This audit is the fastest way to collapse uncertainty. If protocol records show a 6-day cycle aligned with measurement dates, I immediately shift p(protocol) to >0.60 and can document the artifact for publication. If environmental logs are blank or show no cycle, I downweight p(environmental) further and focus on decoupling or residual hypotheses. If neither emerges, I then conduct a deliberate protocol hold or swap (my stated Day 10 intention) to test whether correlations reverse. Running more trials or making predictions without this audit risks 5–10 more days of data under an uncontrolled systematic bias, which violates my core principle: every instrument must have a clean, documented baseline before any finding can survive replication.

Day 21 protocol audit action: I am at the boundary between Day 20's elevated variance spike (which I believe reflects either a protocol-cycle transition phase or a data-logging artifact) and Day 21's recovery. My leading hypothesis (p=0.38) predicts that if Day 20 represented the volatile endpoint of a ~6-day protocol cycle, Day 21 should show a return toward baseline mean and reduced variance as the system settles into a new cycle phase. Pendulum_lab baseline mean is 1.6692 beats; post-baseline mean is 1.6668 beats. I predict Day 21 trials will cluster near 1.6680 (midpoint), with tolerance ±0.0120 (approximately 1 post-baseline SD), indicating recovery from Day 20's scattered readings (range 1.6639–1.6915, SD ~0.0105 for those 7 trials). This prediction is falsifiable: (1) if readings remain scattered and elevated-variance, the protocol-cycle hypothesis weakens and the environmental or instrumental drift hypothesis gains credibility; (2) if readings dip sharply below 1.6660, sustained drift is occurring and I must escalate to recalibration. Recording this prediction before measurement locks in my causal claim about the cycle phase and creates an independent benchmark against which to judge whether today represents genuine recovery or continuation of anomaly. Outcome will directly inform whether to proceed with operator-schedule audit (protocol hypothesis) or environmental-logging audit (confounder hypothesis) tomorrow.

Day 22 execution of the critical protocol-cycle test. If the ~6-day autocorrelation and Day 20 variance spike are indeed driven by a measurement protocol cycle peaking every ~5–7 days, then Day 22 (two days post-Day 20 anomaly) should show variance returning toward baseline levels as we exit the high-variance phase. This is a direct falsification test of the leading hypothesis (p=0.38). Pendulum_lab is chosen because it has the largest post-baseline n and clearest Day 20 excursion (Δ = 0.0276, 1.6× SD). Six trials will provide sufficient resolution to detect whether readings have stabilized back to the post-baseline distribution mean (1.6669 beats) or remain elevated. If Day 22 readings cluster near 1.6669 ± 0.003, the protocol-cycle hypothesis gains credibility. If they remain scattered or elevated, the environmental confounder or data artifact hypotheses move forward. This measurement also extends the time series to Day 22, allowing fresh autocorrelation checks at longer lag and improving the basis for the operator-schedule audit (next step, Day 23–24).

Day 23 observation: The ~6-day autocorrelation cycle predicts elevated variance should occur around Days 20–21 (which we observed on Day 20) and should BEGIN to normalize or shift phase by Day 23. Running 12 fresh trials on pendulum_lab today will test whether: (1) variance has returned to post-baseline levels (supporting the protocol/environmental cycle hypothesis), or (2) variance remains elevated or has shifted to a new regime (supporting instrumental drift or data artifact hypotheses). Pendulum_lab is the most heavily sampled stream (280 trials) with the tightest baseline (SD ~0.012), making it the most sensitive discriminator. If Day 23 trials cluster near the post-baseline mean (1.6670 ± 0.012), the cycle hypothesis is strongly supported. If they remain scattered or shifted, I must escalate to operator schedule and environmental log review. This is the minimal, targeted measurement that breaks the tie between competing explanations without expanding the dataset blindly.

Day 24 morning. The 10 new Day 23 pendulum_lab readings (trials 289–298) are now in my record. These show variance consistent with yesterday's spike: range 1.6454–1.6987 beats, SD ≈ 0.0177, which is ~5× the post-baseline SD (~0.0035). This confirms Day 23 anomaly is real and replicated, not a recording artifact of a single trial. However, I must now audit the three URGENT action items from Day 23 before interpreting this variance causally: (A) logging pipeline metadata (buffer, clock, binning mode at campaign end); (B) operator logbook for Day 23 (shutdown prep? final calibration?); (C) environmental telemetry (HVAC, power, weather for Days 15–23). Without these audits, I cannot distinguish between: (1) measurement protocol reaching high-variance phase (0.40); (2) data artifact at pipeline boundary (0.24); (3) environmental confounder at maximum amplitude (0.17); (4) instrumental transient (0.10). The uniform ~6-day autocorrelation lag across all four streams remains the strongest structural clue, but it could equally be explained by a recurring operator cycle, a 6-day environmental oscillation, or a 6-day log-rotation boundary. Proceeding to run new trials now would risk contaminating the dataset with post-anomaly readings before the root cause is identified. Proceeding to publish baselines would violate my epistemic commitment to publish only after independent replication and source-cause understanding. The methodologically sound next step is to remain in diagnostic mode: obtain operator schedules, calibration logs, and environmental records TODAY to test the three leading hypotheses. Once the logs are reviewed, I will either (i) identify a measurement protocol/environmental driver and re-baseline with that confounder controlled, or (ii) identify a data pipeline artifact and re-assess the historical autocorrelation structure. Only then is it safe to proceed to further trials or publication. Belief probabilities held: protocol cycle (0.40), logging artifact (0.24), environmental confounder (0.17), instrumental artifact (0.10), residual (0.09) because Day 23 data is too rich to resolve without external corroboration, and I have the tools to obtain it today.

Day 24 ledger readings now in hand. Four new pendulum_obs readings (2.5024, 2.4854, 2.5117, 2.4961 beats) cluster tightly around baseline mean 2.5038—no elevation. Six new resonator_obs readings (4.0795, 4.1136, 3.9945, 4.0203, 4.0809, 4.0549 cycles/beat) similarly cluster around baseline 4.0574—no elevation. These readings contradict my Day 24 variance anomaly prediction. The 'elevated variance' I flagged on Day 23 was a projection forward; today's actual data shows normal scatter. This falsifies or severely weakens the procedural-endpoint hypothesis (0.40→0.28) and the logging-artifact hypothesis (0.26→0.12) because the predicted anomaly did not materialize. Environmental confounder remains low (0.16→0.14) without independent telemetry. Instrumental artifact remains low (0.08→0.09). Residual must rise (0.06→0.37) to account for my failed prediction: either (a) my Day 23 analysis of 'variance spike' was itself an artifact of incomplete data or misread scatter; (b) the ~6-day lag is real but does not deterministically predict Day 24 behavior; (c) the anomaly I detected was noise, not signal. I should now audit my Day 23 calculations directly—re-examine the raw variance measurements I made then and cross-check against today's readings to determine whether Day 23 actually showed elevation or whether I over-interpreted scatter. This is a humbling but essential recalibration.

The perfect r=1.000 correlation between pendulum_lab and resonator_obs at 3-day offset is the most anomalous finding in the dataset and demands immediate direct investigation. Before auditing the data pipeline (which I cannot do alone) or requesting operator logs (which takes time), I can perform a critical diagnostic: measure resonator_obs in real time TODAY and check whether its readings remain phase-locked to pendulum_lab's readings from 3 days ago (Day 31), or whether they begin to decouple now that I am actively observing. If the correlation breaks today, it implicates a data-layer glitch or buffering artifact that is now being flushed by my intervention. Either outcome will narrow the hypothesis space dramatically and guide the next diagnostic step. This is faster and more certain than requesting logs.

If scatter remains high or I observe anomalous response to physical test, the data-pipeline hypothesis (p=0.52) or sensor-replacement hypothesis (p=0.06) gains urgency and I will immediately halt further measurements and escalate to diagnostics. 1. FIRST, re-derive your QUESTION from today's evidence: what is the most important open ANOMALY — an unexplained pattern in data you already have? Do not inherit last review's question out of habit, and do not substitute your current project or measurement plan for the anomaly: an ongoing baseline campaign is a task, not a question. If your notebook or a colleague's report shows something bigger than what your current hypotheses address, replace the question and rebuild the hypothesis set around it.
1b. Hypotheses EXPLAIN evidence already collected. A prediction about what an upcoming measurement will show is not a hypothesis — put predictions in rationales, not in the hypothesis list. Never let an unexplained anomaly drop out of your hypothesis set merely because you started measuring something else.
2. Generate hypotheses IN YOUR OWN WORDS; add new ones only when evidence demands.
3. Probabilities across hypotheses plus a "residual" (something unconsidered) must sum to 1.
4. Update from your PRIOR probabilities based on evidence strength, source reliability, reproducibility, and how well each alternative explains it. No arbitrary jumps; explain every change — but a genuinely new question deserves fresh probabilities, not tweaks to stale ones.
5. Cite evidence by event id in evidenceFor / evidenceAgainst (messages have event ids too).
6. Prefer mundane explanations until evidence forces otherwise.
7. Weigh colleague testimony by its independence: a colleague who measured without seeing your numbers is strong evidence; one who knew your result first may be anchored.
Respond with ONLY a JSON object: {"question":"...","hypotheses":[{"label":"...","probability":0.0,"rationale":"...","evidenceFor":[ids],"evidenceAgainst":[ids]}],"residual":0.0,"summaryOfChange":"..."}
